To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) we unify recent neural approaches with older ideas of Hebbian learning and associative memory in a metalearning model; (2) our model builds representations via slow, task-averaged weights, while fast weights, constructed by a Hebbing learning rule, implement one-shot learning of class labels; (3) our model achieves state of the art results on the Omniglot and Mini-ImageNet benchmarks; (4) we show that our model can also be applied to language learning

we propose a novel metalearning approach that unifies recent neural approaches to few-shot learning with older Hebbian ideas of associative memory, that we achieve state-of-the-art performance on one-shot learning benchmarks for images, words and symbols, and that we show that the model can learn to solve new tasks with a single example.
We propose a new model for meta-learning that combines recent ideas of one-shot learning and older ideas of associative binding in a single model.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions: (i) How do neural circuits learn and store information about new tasks? (ii) How do neural networks learn and store new concepts and representations?
the following questions: (1) Can we learn to learn? (2) Can we learn from a few examples? (3) What is the role of attention? (4) Can we build an intelligent machine?
the question of how to learn to learn.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the proposed approach is the state of the art on one shot learning.
this paper presents a novel model that unifies the ideas of associative memory and metalearning.
the proposed metalearning approach with Hebbian fast weights achieves state-of-the art performance on one-shot learning benchmarks.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we unify recent neural approaches with older ideas of memory in a model which is able to perform one-shot learning.
we unify recent approaches to one-shot and few-shot learning with older models for associative learning and memory.
we unify recent approaches to few-shot learning with older ones of associative memory in meta-learning.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the same Hebbian fast weights that underlie associative learning in the brain may also be the key to learning in artificial neural networks.
fast weights are a powerful tool for learning with one-shot data.
the same fast weight learning rule that underlies the associative memory of Hopfield nets also underlies the fast learning of one-shot learning.
